meta.theme: the demand for evidence that a policy works is three demands, that the effect is real, that it will be reproduced by the machinery available here, and that the result is the one wanted, of which only the first is answered by trials and the third is not an evidential question at all, so the characteristic misuse of the phrase is to close a disagreement about objectives with a demonstration of effects

meta.reviewer_notes: Heavily signposted, which is what keeps a long passage at this stage: first, second and third are named and kept in order. The difficulty is entirely in not letting the three merge, and four of the five questions are decided by sorting a statement into the right one of the three. The closing paragraph is a concession, and the role-of-detail question is built on readers who take it for a change of position. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 625→499 words, 5→5 paragraphs, 5→4 questions. Each of the five paragraphs is one of the numbered parts or the fence round the complaint, so tightened all five instead of dropping one; dropped q5 (role of detail), which shared its paragraph with the inference question.

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option that a bigger and more precise trial would settle the case, which is true about measurement and beside the point about the exchange: the passage says a study reports how many of each and nothing whatever about how many of one are worth one of the other, because that is not a fact about the rule. Q2's rival is the option that the second question is what trials are built to answer, which is a true sentence about the first question docked at the wrong number. Q3's rival is the option that the phrase was introduced in order to conceal disagreements about objectives, which converts a described abuse into an original purpose; the fifth paragraph credits the demand with displacing ministerial confidence and calls it an enormous improvement. Q4's rival is the title about rescuing policy from intuition, which names the concession rather than the argument. Q5's rival is the option that the recollection is there as the history of a phrase, which mistakes a defensive move for a narrative one. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q5 was dropped, so any note above about it no longer applies.)

paragraphs.text: What is a person asking for when he asks whether there is evidence that a policy works? The question sounds like one demand and it is three. The first is whether the effect is real: whether the thing, somewhere, under some conditions, produced the result attributed to it. The second is whether it will be produced here, by the staff, the buildings and the habits that this administration actually has. The third is whether the result is the one we wanted, weighed against the other results the same money and attention might have bought.

Only the first is an evidential question in the narrow sense, and it is the one that trials were designed to settle. They settle it well. A comparison between groups sorted by something unrelated to the outcome will tell you whether the difference between them was caused by what you did, and a generation of careful work has made such comparisons harder to fake. When the phrase evidence-based is used precisely, this is what it names, and there is nothing wrong with it.

The second question is administrative, and no trial answers it, because a trial runs with the attention it was given and a programme runs with the attention it can get. Yet it is a question about resemblance, and it can be argued about with evidence of a different kind: what this department has sustained before, how long its last scheme kept its staff. Whoever asks for such records is asking for evidence quite as properly as whoever asks for a trial.

The third question is not an evidential question at all, and no number of trials will make it one. Consider a rule that lowers the number of dangerous people released and raises the number of harmless people detained. A good study will tell you how many of each, and nothing whatever about how many of the second are worth one of the first, because that is not a fact about the rule. It is a judgement about what we owe to two sets of people whose interests are opposed. Here the phrase does its damage. It promises all three answers and delivers one, and its characteristic abuse is not falsifying a figure but answering the first question when the disagreement is plainly of the third kind, so that a dispute about what we want is closed by a demonstration of what works.

None of this is an argument against asking for evidence. Before the demand, a scheme was adopted because a minister was confident, because the department had always done it, or because somebody told a story that hung together well, and an answer to the first question is an enormous improvement on any of them. The complaint is narrower: a phrase that names one of three questions should not be allowed to stand for all three. The sign of misuse is easy to describe: it appears when a disagreement about objectives appears, and not when a disagreement about effects does.

questions.target_mistake: reaching for more measurement when the parties already agree about the measurements and disagree about what they are worth
questions.prediction_target: The learner should sort the case before reading the options: both sides accept the effects, so the dispute cannot belong to the first question and must belong to the third.
questions.stem: Two officials agree that a proposed scheme lowers the number of missed diagnoses and raises the number of healthy people sent for further tests, and they disagree about whether to adopt it. On the author's account, their disagreement

options.A: belongs to the second question, and should be settled by the department's record with similar schemes
options.B: shows that one of them has misread the study, since both effects have already been measured
options.C: belongs to the third question and cannot be closed by any further trial, however well conducted
options.D: could be resolved by a larger study measuring each of the two effects more precisely

explanation.expert_notice: The case is built from the passage's own example with the terms changed. Both parties accept the two effects, which removes the first question, and neither is disputing whether this department could run the scheme, which removes the second. What is left is an exchange rate between two kinds of harm falling on two sets of people.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option sorts the disagreement into the third question and takes the consequence the passage attaches to it. A study reports how many of each effect and says nothing about how many of one are worth one of the other, because that is not a fact about the rule but a judgement about what is owed to people whose interests are opposed. No trial, of any size, produces such a number.
explanation.question_type_note: An application question wants the author's rule run on a case he never saw. Extract the rule as a rule and check the new case against each of its parts before reading the options.
explanation.reading_habit: When a dispute is described, ask first what the parties already agree about. What they agree about tells you which question they are not having, and that usually leaves only one.

distractors.why_wrong: The second question is whether the effect will be reproduced by the machinery available here, and nobody in the case doubts that it will. The records the third paragraph recommends answer a question about resemblance, which is not the one in dispute.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does urge that administrative records count as evidence, and an option recommending them sounds like the author's own practical advice.

distractors.why_wrong: This treats the disagreement as factual when the passage has just explained that it cannot be. Both officials accept the same figures; what they differ over is what the figures are worth, and the passage insists that this is not something the study contains.
distractors.seductive_element: Where two people disagree after seeing the same evidence, the natural first thought is that one of them has read it badly.

distractors.why_wrong: Greater precision improves the answer to the first question, which is not the one being asked. The passage says a good study tells you how many of each and nothing whatever about the rate at which one trades against the other.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because more and better measurement is the standard remedy in disputes about policy and the option concedes that both effects are real.

questions.target_mistake: attaching to the second question a description the passage gives of the first or the third
questions.stem: According to the passage, the second of the three questions

options.A: asks whether the effect will be produced by the staff and habits this administration has
options.B: is the one that trials were designed to settle, and a generation of work has made them better at it
options.C: cannot be argued about by producing evidence of any kind whatever
options.D: is answered once a scheme has been shown to work in more than one place

explanation.expert_notice: The first paragraph numbers the three and defines each in a sentence, and the three middle paragraphs then take them in order. The second is introduced as whether the effect will be produced here, by the staff, the buildings and the habits that this administration actually has.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that definition. The third paragraph confirms it by explaining why a trial cannot answer it, since a trial runs with the attention it was given and a programme with the attention it can get, and by naming the kind of record that can: what this department has sustained before, and how its last scheme fared.
explanation.question_type_note: When a passage numbers its parts, detail questions are usually built by moving a true statement from one number to another. Check which part each option is describing before checking whether it is true.
explanation.reading_habit: In a passage organised as a list, write the list down in three or four words per item. The list is what the questions are made of, and reconstructing it from memory is where readers go wrong.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second paragraph's description of the first question, which it calls the only evidential question in the narrow sense and the one trials were designed to settle. The passage says expressly that no trial answers the second.
distractors.seductive_element: It is a true sentence of the passage, and the word second appears in the stem while the paragraph describing trials is itself the second one.

distractors.why_wrong: This belongs to the third question, and even there the passage's claim is narrower. What it says of the second is the opposite: it can be argued about with evidence of a different kind, and whoever asks for such records is asking for evidence quite as properly as anyone else.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does say no trial answers the second question, and a reader who remembers only that half will hear a general refusal of evidence.

distractors.why_wrong: Replication in several places is never mentioned. The second question is about the particular administration that will run the scheme, so results obtained elsewhere are exactly what it declines to treat as settling the matter.
distractors.seductive_element: Working in more than one place is the familiar test of whether a finding travels, and it sounds like the natural answer to a question about reproduction.

questions.target_mistake: converting a described misuse of the phrase into the purpose for which the phrase was introduced
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict from the closing sign: the appeal is suspect when it arrives with a disagreement about objectives, which is exactly when the effects are not in dispute.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: A policy supported by good trials is more likely to be adopted than one that is not supported by any.
options.B: The demand for evidence was taken up in the first place as a way of hiding disagreements about objectives.
options.C: An appeal to evidence deserves most suspicion when the parties already agree about what the scheme does.
options.D: Questions of the third kind arise only where a scheme is shown to produce two opposed effects at once.

explanation.expert_notice: The last sentence gives a test rather than a complaint: the sign of misuse is that the appeal appears when a disagreement about objectives appears, and not when a disagreement about effects does. The fourth paragraph has already described the manoeuvre, which is to answer the first question while the argument is of the third kind.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option states that test from the other side. A dispute in which both parties accept what the scheme does is by definition not a dispute about effects, so an appeal to evidence there can only be answering a question nobody is asking. The passage supplies both halves: the abuse it names and the sign by which it says the abuse can be recognised.
explanation.question_type_note: Where an author ends by giving a sign or a symptom, the inference question usually asks for the same sign expressed as a condition. Read the final sentence twice before the options.
explanation.reading_habit: Turn a stated warning into a question you could ask in the room. An author who says when a move is suspect has told you what to look for, and the inference is that observation restated.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage never discusses which policies get adopted. It is about what a demand for evidence amounts to and how an answer to one question is used to close another, which leaves the fate of well-supported schemes entirely open.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like a modest and safe claim, and modest claims are often correct in inference questions.

distractors.why_wrong: A described abuse has been converted into an original motive. The fifth paragraph says the opposite about the demand's origins, crediting it with displacing ministerial confidence and departmental habit and calling it an enormous improvement.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the fourth paragraph really does describe the phrase being used to close a dispute about objectives, and a reader who has that manoeuvre in mind will accept an account of why it exists.

distractors.why_wrong: The two opposed effects are one illustration of the third question, not its condition. The first paragraph defines that question as whether the result is the one wanted, weighed against the other results the same money and attention might have bought.
distractors.seductive_element: The only worked case in the passage has exactly this shape, and a reader who takes the example for the rule will find the restriction natural.

questions.target_mistake: titling the passage from the paragraph that concedes, or from the single question the passage spends least time defending
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the title must carry the division of one demand into three, because every paragraph after the first is one of the three or a defence of the division.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: The Limits of What a Department Can Deliver
options.C: How Policy Was Rescued from Intuition

explanation.expert_notice: The first paragraph announces the structure of the whole piece: the question sounds like one demand and it is three. The three middle paragraphs take them in order, and the last says the complaint is that one phrase has been allowed to stand for all three.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title names the division and nothing else, which is what the passage argues for. It reaches the paragraph on trials, the paragraph on administration and the paragraph on objectives, because each is one of the three, and it leaves room for the closing concession, which grants the phrase its value in the one question it properly names.
explanation.question_type_note: A title is the main idea under a word limit. Where a passage divides one thing into parts, the title has to keep the division; a title naming a single part has named a paragraph.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask which paragraphs a candidate title would leave with nothing to do. The right title is the one under which every paragraph is still earning its place.

distractors.why_wrong: This names the second question alone, which occupies one paragraph and is the one the passage treats most briskly. The paragraph that carries the argument is the fourth, about the question no evidence answers.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the most concrete of the four and describes a real and recognisable problem that the passage does discuss at some length.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the fifth paragraph's concession, granted in order to keep the complaint from being read as a general attack. Taken as the title it would make the passage an appreciation of a movement the passage is in fact trying to discipline.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because that paragraph is warmly written and contains the passage's only piece of praise, which reads like a verdict.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage's point about the third question is that what matters most cannot be measured at all, so a title promising to measure it inverts the argument while sounding like a summary of it.
distractors.seductive_element: It has the cadence of a policy essay's title and borrows the vocabulary of measurement that runs through the whole piece.

vocabulary.passage_use: an evidential question in the narrow sense
vocabulary.meaning_here: capable of being settled by finding out what is the case

vocabulary.passage_use: It is a question about resemblance
vocabulary.meaning_here: how far the new setting is like the one the result came from

mentor.challenge: One question is split into three in the first paragraph, and the rest of the passage takes them in order. Keep the numbers straight; almost every question in the set is decided by which of the three a sentence belongs to.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Asking whether there is evidence that a policy works is really asking three different things, whether the effect is real, whether this administration will reproduce it, and whether the result is the one we wanted, of which trials answer only the first and the third is not an evidential question at all, so the phrase does its damage when it is produced to close a disagreement about objectives with a demonstration of effects.
mentor.main_idea: The demand for evidence bundles three questions. Trials answer the first, about whether the effect is real. The second, about whether this administration can reproduce it, is answered by records of what the department has sustained before. The third, about whether the result is worth its cost to others, is not answerable by evidence at all, because it asks what is owed to people whose interests conflict. The phrase promises all three and delivers one, and its misuse is recognisable: it appears when the disagreement is about objectives.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Somebody says: show me the evidence that this policy works. That sounds like one request. It is really three.

The first is: did this thing actually produce the result somewhere? The second is: will it produce that result here, with the people and buildings and habits this particular department has? The third is: is that result the one we actually want, once you weigh it against what the same money and attention could have bought instead?

Only the first is a question that trials answer, and they answer it well. Compare two groups sorted in a way unrelated to the outcome, and you can say whether your intervention made the difference. When people use the phrase evidence-based carefully, this is what they mean, and it is a good thing.

The second question is about administration, not about the intervention. A trial runs with the attention it was given; a national programme runs with whatever attention it can get. That is not hopeless, though. You can argue about it with a different sort of evidence: what this department has kept going before, whether its last scheme held on to its staff. Boring records, but real evidence.

The third question is different in kind. Suppose a rule releases fewer dangerous people and also locks up more harmless ones. A good study tells you how many of each. It cannot tell you how many wrongly detained people are worth one dangerous person kept in, because that is not a fact about the rule at all. It is a judgement about what we owe two groups whose interests clash.

And this is where the phrase does harm. It promises answers to all three questions and delivers one. The typical abuse is not faking numbers. It is producing an answer to the first question at the exact moment when the argument is obviously about the third, so that a disagreement about what we want gets settled by a demonstration of what works.

The author is careful to add that none of this means we should stop asking for evidence. Before the demand existed, schemes were adopted because a minister felt sure, or because it was always done that way, or because someone told a convincing story. Compared with those, an answer to the first question is an enormous improvement. The complaint is narrow: one phrase should not be allowed to stand for three questions, and you can spot the misuse easily, because it turns up when people disagree about goals rather than when they disagree about effects.
mentor.why_difficult: The difficulty is not in any one sentence but in keeping three numbered things apart across five paragraphs. Most wrong options in the set are true statements about one of the three attached to another, and under time those migrations are very hard to catch, especially since the paragraph describing trials happens to be the second paragraph while the question it describes is the first. The other trap is the closing paragraph, which concedes generously and reads like a change of position, so that readers take the concession for the thesis or take the whole passage for an attack on evidence, which it says twice that it is not.
mentor.author_intention: To break a single slogan into the three demands it conceals, so that a reader can see which of them any particular appeal to evidence has actually answered, and then to stop that analysis being used as a licence to ignore evidence altogether.

paragraph_journey.note: Asking for evidence is three requests: is the effect real, will it happen here with these people, and is the result the one we wanted.
This is the one trials were built for, and they do it well. Used precisely, the phrase evidence-based names this and nothing more.
Administrative, and no trial reaches it, since a trial has the attention it was given. But records of what the department has sustained before are evidence too.
Not evidential at all. A study counts both effects and cannot say what one is worth against the other, because that is a judgement about what we owe people who disagree.
This is not an attack on evidence: the alternatives were a confident minister and a good story. The complaint is only that one phrase must not stand for three questions.

mentor.tone_progression: It begins in the patient voice of someone making a distinction, stays level and technical through the first two answers, sharpens into something close to indignation at the moment the phrase is said to do its damage, and then deliberately cools, spending its last paragraph giving ground it did not have to give.
key_transitions: 'The question sounds like one demand and it is three' (paragraph 1): the whole structure of the passage is set in a single clause.
'The third question is not an evidential question at all' (opening of paragraph 4): the argument arrives at the claim the earlier paragraphs were preparing.
'None of this is an argument against asking for evidence' (opening of paragraph 5): the author fences his own complaint before anyone else can widen it.
mentor.misunderstanding: Two readings go wrong. The first collapses the three questions into a general suspicion of trials, so the passage becomes an attack on evidence in policy, which its second paragraph and its last both refuse. The second keeps the three questions but loses their order, which is easy because the paragraph about trials is the second paragraph while the question it answers is the first; from there a reader will confidently attach the wrong description to the wrong number. The signposting looks generous and is the very thing that makes the migration invisible.
mentor.traps_summary: This set moves true statements between the three numbered questions, offers more measurement where the dispute is not about measurement, converts a described abuse into an original purpose, and takes the concession as the thesis. Numbering the three questions in your own words before starting answers most of them.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author numbers his parts, write the list down in a few words each and keep it beside you, because in passages of this shape the distractors are almost never false statements: they are true statements filed under the wrong number. Then watch for the paragraph that begins by saying what the author is not arguing, and treat everything in it as a fence rather than as a retreat, since the questions on such passages are built on readers who take a concession for a conclusion.
mentor.real_world: The same three questions sit under any appeal to what the research shows: a school method, a management technique, a drug, a piece of software procurement. Asking which of the three a study has answered is usually enough to change the conversation.
mentor.takeaway: A trial can tell you what a policy does; it cannot tell you whether what it does is what you wanted.
mentor.reflection_question: When you last settled an argument by producing evidence, was the disagreement really about what would happen, or about what ought to?

eli10.big_idea: Asking for evidence that a policy works is really three questions, and trials answer only one; the third is about what we want.
eli10.story: Someone says, 'Show me the evidence that this plan works.' It sounds like one question. The writer says it is three. First: did it really work somewhere? Second: will it work here, with our people and habits? Third: is the result what we want? Fair tests (trials comparing two groups) answer the first well. The second needs a different kind of proof, like the department's past record. The third is not about facts at all. Imagine a rule that keeps more dangerous people locked up but also locks up more harmless people. A study can count both groups. It cannot say how many harmless people are worth one dangerous one. That is about what we owe people. The trouble starts when someone answers the first question to shut down an argument about the third. Still, the writer is not against evidence. It beats a minister's hunch or a good story.
paragraphs: Splits one question into three: did it work, will it work here, and is it what we want?
Answers the first: fair trials settle whether an effect is real, and they do it well.
Answers the second: trials cannot, but a department's past record is real evidence too.
Says the third is not about facts at all, and shows how the phrase gets misused there.
Heads off a misreading: evidence beats hunches, but one phrase must not stand for three questions.
eli10.author_view: The writer is patient and precise, gets sharp about the misuse, and stays fair to evidence itself.
